title: Element Interactivity
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark's second edition in the DistillED series on cognitive load theory explains element interactivity, the degree to which the pieces of a task depend on one another and must be held in working memory together. He separates it from difficulty and from a fixed property of content, since what overloads a novice can be a single familiar chunk for an expert. He draws on Ashman, Kalyuga and Sweller (2020) and Zhang and Sweller (2024) to show that explicit instruction first suits students with less knowledge, while investigation first becomes workable as knowledge grows. He also notes that retrieval practice pays off most with lower-interactivity material. The practical half is a five-step planning routine: separate parts from connections, check what is secure, pre-teach the parts, model the whole, and hand over as knowledge grows. A density sequence in physics shows the same content being taught differently as pupils' knowledge changes.
points: Element interactivity is about how many parts depend on each other, not how hard or long a task is, so a short but tightly connected task can overload working memory more than a long list of separate facts.
Because the measure depends on prior knowledge, the same lesson can sit in a different place for different classes, and a quick judgement or knowledge check is enough to place it.

The explain-first versus try-first debate depends on the meeting point of content and class: students with less knowledge do better with explicit instruction first, and investigation pays off once more of the parts are secure.
Pre-teaching the individual terms, symbols and steps before combining them frees working memory for the connections that matter.
Retrieval practice works best when the material is lower in element interactivity, so complex content usually needs modelling before it is ready to be retrieved.
quotes: Element interactivity describes how much the pieces of information in a task depend on one another. When they interact, students must process them simultaneously in working memory to make sense of the task.

Learning a thousand French nouns is hard work, but it is hard because there are so many of them. Each noun can still be learned on its own, so each one places relatively little strain on working memory.

A later study with 85 middle school students learning about density added nuance. Among students with at least some secure prior knowledge, those who knew less did better with explicit instruction first, while those who knew more did better investigating first.
This is also why difficulty can mislead us. We tend to slow down for topics that feel big and rush the ones that look small.

You can't see inside your students’ heads, and you don't need to. Researchers can count the elements in a task, but what students already know can only be estimated, through teacher judgement or quick knowledge checks
Teach and retrieve the terms, symbols or steps separately first. When students meet the full task, each part is already secure and working memory is free for the connections.
Notice what changed across that sequence. The content stayed the same. What students knew grew, and so the teaching shifted with it.
